introduction: These are hard pages. Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá look at the decline of Islam, and of Shí‘ih Islam in Iran above all, and name its causes: division, traditions and tales taken for the faith, a clergy that fed on its flock, pride in being the saved community, centuries of cursing from the pulpit, and at last the killing of the very One for whom the community had prayed. The purpose is stated near the end: “Do not afflict yourselves as did the party of the Shí‘ih.” The history is a mirror held up to the next community. The outside quotations show how old this kind of speech is and that it has always been spoken first to one’s own. Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos and Lamentations say it of Israel; Jesus says it of the scribes and of Jerusalem; the Qur’án says it of the People of the Book and warns the Muslims not to follow them; Paul turns it on Gentile Christians. Gibbon is here for an outsider’s account of ‘Alí, Ḥusayn, the hidden Imám and the long quarrel, with Dostoevsky’s Grand Inquisitor, Milton, Kipling and Tagore. A few passages ask the reader to weigh the readings’ own severity.
questions: The readings say the cause of decline “remaineth unknown and hidden from all” and then name it. What do they say it was? Compare the Qur’án: God does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.
A community that “awaited through nights and days” attacked the One it awaited. The Gospels tell the same of Jerusalem. What is it about long expectation that prepares people to reject?
Traditions are called a cause of ruin; Chesterton calls tradition the democracy of the dead. What distinguishes handing on a faith from covering it?

“They weep for Ḥusayn while they slay his children,” and Jesus speaks of those who build the prophets’ tombs. How can honouring past martyrs coexist with repeating the crime, and how would one notice?

Bahá’u’lláh tells his own followers that some of them “walk in the footsteps of that people.” Paul tells Christians, “be not highminded, but fear.” Which of the faults described here could appear in a Bahá’í community, and what would the early signs be?

The language of these readings about a named community is severe, as is that of the Hebrew prophets and of Jesus about theirs. The Qur’án says, “Let not a folk deride a folk who may be better than they.” How should such passages be read and shared today?

outside.why: The sayings and doings of a community dulled what it had at first. The letter to the church at Ephesus: thou hast left thy first love; remember therefore from whence thou art fallen.
A country in ruins “until justice and equity become its foundation.” Isaiah over Jerusalem: how is the faithful city become an harlot! it was full of judgment; righteousness lodged in it.

What is heard about Islam is “from traditions or relates to branches and details,” not the foundation. Jesus to the teachers of his own religion: making the word of God of none effect through your tradition.
“This weakness hath come about solely due to the differences.” The Qur’án had warned the first Muslims in those terms: dispute not one with another lest ye falter and your strength depart from you.
“The station of Islam hath declined … and the banners have been reversed.” Lamentations: how is the gold become dim! how is the most fine gold changed!
The cause of the weakness “remaineth unknown and hidden.” The Qur’án places it within: Allah changeth not the condition of a folk until they first change that which is in their hearts.
A thousand sorrows, “all being the results of deeds and actions.” The Qur’án: corruption doth appear on land and sea because of that which men’s hands have done.
“Everyone snatches away one of its members, and none can prevent it.” A psalm from an earlier ruin: O God, the heathen are come into thine inheritance; we are become a reproach to our neighbours.
“What happened to that power and strength?” A mother in Israel named her child for the answer: Ichabod, the glory is departed.

The readings look for a moral cause. Byron saw one cycle in every nation, whatever its faith: first freedom, and then glory; when that fails, wealth, vice, corruption, barbarism at last. Is the decline described here a judgment, or the common course of empires?
“Perhaps God will assist … to revive what has been obliterated.” The last prayer of Lamentations: turn thou us unto thee, O Lord, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old.
The same drift in another religion: Christ upheld the Ten Commandments, and the churches filled with images. The commandment: thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image.
Captivated by “the arts and wonders of the West,” they forgot the Causer of Causes. Wordsworth, from inside that West: the world is too much with us; getting and spending, we lay waste our powers.
Good intention, “but they are inert, not active.” James: as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.
A great hospital in Damascus, “now all of it is in ruins.” Shelley’s traveller in the desert: nothing beside remains.
Schooling narrowed to religious disputes. Hosea: my people are destroyed for lack of knowledge.
Chastity must not be made a bar to learning. Mary Wollstonecraft in 1792: strengthen the female mind by enlarging it, and there will be an end to blind obedience.

The fast “has become only a habit … a dead institution.” Isaiah put the same charge and gave the meaning back: is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to let the oppressed go free.

A creed that promises salvation for a sentence publicly confessed. Jesus: not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls salvation by confession a dogma that “has nothing to do with Islam.” Paul appears to teach something like it: if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart, thou shalt be saved. What does Paul add to the words of the mouth, and is that enough to meet the objection?
Traditions “have been the cause of ruin for many homes.” Jesus: laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men.

Tradition as a source of division and calamity. Chesterton defended it as fairness to those who came before: tradition means giving votes to the most obscure of all classes, our ancestors; it is the democracy of the dead. What separates a tradition that carries a faith from one that buries it?
Corruption comes from “the ignorant one who appeareth in the guise of knowledge.” Jesus: beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing.
“The transgressor who is known and seen in the garb of piety.” Jesus: ye are like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward.
After the eleventh Imám the community split into three. Corinth, within a generation of Christ: every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas. Is Christ divided?
The Shí‘ih belief about ‘Alí is reported. An English historian with no stake in the quarrel gave his own estimate of the man: he united the qualifications of a poet, a soldier, and a saint.
The belief that the twelfth Imám disappeared and lives on, as Gibbon set it down for European readers in 1788: his votaries pretend that he still lives, and will appear before the day of judgment.
Where is the Ass of Antichrist, the Sufyán, the conquest of East and West? Jesus was asked for such a timetable and refused it: the kingdom of God cometh not with observation.
The Manifestation does not appear “in conformity with” what people have imagined. Isaiah: my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways.
They honour the House, the Book and the Prophet because each is God’s, and reject the next thing that is God’s. Jerusalem: we are Moses’ disciples; as for this fellow, we know not from whence he is.
“What fruit” did their claims yield on the Day itself? Jesus to the keepers of the vineyard: the kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof.

“What benefit did the Shí‘ihs derive from what they claimed?” The Qur’án to every community that relies on its name: it will not be in accordance with your desires, nor the desires of the People of the Scripture.
“What came of their zealotry?” Paul of his own people: they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge.
“Their lamentations, their seeking and their weeping.” God in Isaiah: when ye make many prayers, I will not hear: your hands are full of blood.
They deemed themselves foremost and “were found to be the most lost.” Jesus: many that are first shall be last; and the last shall be first.
Lives spent on “successor-games.” The First Letter to Timothy: neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions, rather than godly edifying.
“Consider the vainglory.” Kipling warned his own nation at the height of its pride: lest we forget.
“They regarded as unclean the Jews and Christians.” Peter, raised to think the same of Gentiles: God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean.
Each sect holds the next to be the lowest. The Qur’án: the Jews say the Christians follow nothing, and the Christians say the Jews follow nothing; yet both are readers of the Scripture.
“The most learned, most excellent and most God-fearing.” The Pharisee’s prayer: God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are.
They “counted themselves the most excellent of all people.” The Qur’án on the same claim made earlier: we are sons of Allah and His loved ones. Say: nay, ye are but mortals of His creating.
Twelve hundred years of believing themselves the best. Jeremiah at the temple gate: trust ye not in lying words, saying, The temple of the Lord, The temple of the Lord.
“Vain imaginings deprived” them. Bacon: in all superstition wise men follow fools; and arguments are fitted to practice, in a reversed order.
The greatest veil is “the tales that were current amongst you from the imaginings of the ancients.” The Qur’án: we follow that wherein we found our fathers.
For every veil torn, “the people had fashioned for themselves veils thicker.” Plato’s prisoners, shown the fire and the daylight, want their shadows back.

An imaginary being in imaginary cities, defended for a thousand years. The Second Letter to Timothy foresaw it of Christians: they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables.

One community’s sacred history is called a fable. Every community says of its own what the Second Letter of Peter says: we have not followed cunningly devised fables. By what tests can a believer tell, about his own tradition, which it is?
Men of pious appearance “preyed upon the hapless people.” Ezekiel: woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?
The Qur’án of an earlier clergy: many of the rabbis and the monks devour the wealth of mankind wantonly and debar men from the way of Allah.
A man who spoke the truth has been called “the Liar” for twelve centuries. Isaiah: woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light.
The divines maintain the tale, and whoever says otherwise is condemned. Jeremiah: the prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests bear rule by their means; and my people love to have it so.

Traditions that made any claimant an infidel “caused many to be martyred without guilt.” The Qur’án to an earlier people: whenever a messenger cometh with that which ye desire not, some ye disbelieve and some ye slay.
“They curse from their pulpits.” James: therewith bless we God, and therewith curse we men; my brethren, these things ought not so to be.
“Taking illusion as your leader.” The Qur’án: they have taken as lords beside Allah their rabbis and their monks.
They “recite His words at all times” and deny the verses when they come. Isaiah: this people draw near me with their mouth, but have removed their heart far from me.

“Every year in the month of Muḥarram strife ariseth.” What the month remembers moved even Gibbon: in a distant age and climate, the tragic scene of the death of Hosein will awaken the sympathy of the coldest reader. How does grief for a martyr turn into hatred of the living, and what would keep it from doing so?
Such hatred between factions, for twelve hundred years. Gibbon: the religious discord of the friends and enemies of Ali has been renewed in every age of the Hegira.
“Each faction held fast to a cord and clung to a name.” The Qur’án to Muḥammad: as for those who sunder their religion and become schismatics, no concern at all hast thou with them.
“Each faction cursed the other.” Paul: if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another.
Twelve centuries of dispute over what was done in the first. The Qur’án: those are a people who have passed away; ye will not be asked of what they used to do.
“Aflame with the fire of hatred.” The First Letter of John: he that saith he is in the light, and hateth his brother, is in darkness even until now.
“The pulpit was established for the mention of God.” Jesus in the temple: my house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves.
“They awaited through nights and days,” and met him with swords. John: he came unto his own, and his own received him not.
Jesus told it as a story: the owner’s son comes to the vineyard, and the tenants say, this is the heir; come, let us kill him.
They count themselves people of unity and slew the one they prayed for. Stephen to the council: which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted?
“Martyred through the verdict of the … divines.” Dostoevsky imagined Christ returning to Seville and the Grand Inquisitor saying to him: why, then, hast Thou come to hinder us?
At the mention of a name, “the verdict of unbelief, plunder and death.” Jesus: the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service.
Those they despised proved “higher and more excellent.” Jesus to the chief priests: the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you.

They weep for the Prince of Martyrs and curse the One for whom he died. Jesus: ye build the tombs of the prophets, and say, if we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partakers with them.
“They weep for Ḥusayn while they slay his children.” Luke’s version is as short: your fathers killed them, and ye build their sepulchres.
Years of crying “O Truth!” Jesus, weeping over a city that had waited for centuries: thou knewest not the time of thy visitation.

They longed for the Day. Amos warned those who longed for it in his time: woe unto you that desire the day of the Lord! the day of the Lord is darkness, and not light. Why might a community that prays for the Promised One be the least ready to receive him?
They cry “Thirst! Thirst!” and will not go to the water. Jeremiah: they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.
A thousand pilgrims cry “Here am I!” and “hear no response.” God in Amos: I hate, I despise your feast days, and I will not smell in your solemn assemblies.
They “wilfully disregard this knowledge and power.” John: though he had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not on him.
Once the world was awed “by the might of Islam and the power of its kings.” Lamentations: she that was great among the nations, how is she become tributary!
“The standard of Islam lieth prostrate … and its throne is shattered,” and the cause is its own people. Lamentations: the crown is fallen from our head: woe unto us, that we have sinned!
Brought low by those who “cast aside what was sent down.” Judges: there arose another generation after them, which knew not the Lord, nor yet the works which he had done.
When a government tries to bring order, the people and their leaders should support it. Jeremiah to the exiles: seek the peace of the city; for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes “Cling one and all to the Faith of Allah and let nothing divide you.” The verse in Pickthall’s English: hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate.
The counsel was rejected, with the result foretold: every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation.
“Islam must advance through the power of God,” not by militancy. Zechariah: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
The Qur’án’s own word on spreading faith by force: there is no compulsion in religion.
“This power has gone out of the body of Islam.” The Second Letter to Timothy on a religion in that state: having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof.
The letter to the church at Sardis: thou hast a name that thou livest, and art dead.

A rite kept up year after year at the same spot. Tagore to the worshipper in a shut temple: leave this chanting and singing and telling of beads! Is the fault in rites themselves, or in what the readings call forgetting their “higher reasons”?

“Have they not witnessed the fruits?” Bahá’u’lláh now turns the history on his own readers. Paul did the same with Israel’s: these things happened unto them for ensamples; wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.
Some “walk in the footsteps of that people.” Jesus, told of others’ calamities: suppose ye that these were sinners above all? I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.
“Now too the deniers among the Bayán cling to the same vain imaginings.” Paul to Christians inclined to look down on Israel: boast not against the branches; be not highminded, but fear.
The sect “hath been renewed … the same names as before.” Ecclesiastes: the thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and there is no new thing under the sun.
They “reflect not in the least upon … what fruit their beliefs have yielded.” Jesus: ye shall know them by their fruits.
In their turbans “they rush through cities and regions, never failing to lead people astray.” Jesus: ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte.
Milton on the clergy of his own church: the hungry sheep look up, and are not fed.

“Do not afflict yourselves as did the party of the Shí‘ih.” The Qur’án said this to the first Muslims about those before them: that they become not as those who received the Scripture of old, but the term was prolonged for them and so their hearts were hardened.

The lesson is addressed to the “people of God.” Jesus: first cast out the beam out of thine own eye. What would it look like for any community today, a Bahá’í one included, to read these pages as a description of what it could become?
“Ponder their outcome and fruit.” Hosea: they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind.
“Not one among the divines hath been truly aware.” Isaiah: his watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark.
What the office was for. Malachi: the priest’s lips should keep knowledge; but ye are departed out of the way; ye have caused many to stumble.

A believer is congratulated on being purified from a sect. The Qur’án also says: let not a folk deride a folk who may be better than they. How does a reader take the warning in these pages without despising the people they describe?
Those who “cast behind them” the faction and hold to what God loves. Paul: forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before.

gibbon-immortal-hatred-of-persians-and-t.text: The mischiefs that flow from the contests of ambition are usually confined to the times and countries in which they have been agitated. But the religious discord of the friends and enemies of Ali has been renewed in every age of the Hegira, and is still maintained in the immortal hatred of the Persians and Turks
gibbon-immortal-hatred-of-persians-and-t.author: Edward Gibbon
gibbon-immortal-hatred-of-persians-and-t.work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire

gibbon-twelfth-imam-concealed.text: The twelfth and last of the Imams, conspicuous by the title of Mahadi, or the Guide, surpassed the solitude and sanctity of his predecessors. He concealed himself in a cavern near Bagdad: the time and place of his death are unknown; and his votaries pretend that he still lives, and will appear before the day of judgment to overthrow the tyranny of Dejal, or the Antichrist
gibbon-twelfth-imam-concealed.author: Edward Gibbon
gibbon-twelfth-imam-concealed.work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire

gibbon-ali-poet-soldier-saint.text: He united the qualifications of a poet, a soldier, and a saint
gibbon-ali-poet-soldier-saint.author: Edward Gibbon
gibbon-ali-poet-soldier-saint.work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire

samuel-the-glory-is-departed.text: And she named the child Ichabod, saying, The glory is departed from Israel: because the ark of God was taken, and because of her father in law and her husband. And she said, The glory is departed from Israel: for the ark of God is taken

isaiah-how-is-the-faithful-city.text: How is the faithful city become an harlot! it was full of judgment; righteousness lodged in it; but now murderers. Thy silver is become dross, thy wine mixed with water: Thy princes are rebellious, and companions of thieves: every one loveth gifts, and followeth after rewards: they judge not the fatherless, neither doth the cause of the widow come unto them

lamentations-crown-is-fallen.text: The joy of our heart is ceased; our dance is turned into mourning. The crown is fallen from our head: woe unto us, that we have sinned! For this our heart is faint; for these things our eyes are dim

lamentations-how-is-the-gold-become-dim.text: How is the gold become dim! how is the most fine gold changed! the stones of the sanctuary are poured out in the top of every street. The precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, how are they esteemed as earthen pitchers, the work of the hands of the potter

jeremiah-my-people-love-to-have-it-so.text: A wonderful and horrible thing is committed in the land; The prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests bear rule by their means; and my people love to have it so: and what will ye do in the end thereof

jeremiah-pen-of-the-scribes-is-in-vain.text: How do ye say, We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us? Lo, certainly in vain made he it; the pen of the scribes is in vain. The wise men are ashamed, they are dismayed and taken: lo, they have rejected the word of the Lord; and what wisdom is in them

john-we-are-moses-disciples.text: Then they reviled him, and said, Thou art his disciple; but we are Moses' disciples. We know that God spake unto Moses: as for this fellow, we know not from whence he is

john-abraham-is-our-father.text: They answered and said unto him, Abraham is our father. Jesus saith unto them, If ye were Abraham's children, ye would do the works of Abraham. But now ye seek to kill me, a man that hath told you the truth, which I have heard of God: this did not Abraham

peter-cunningly-devised-fables.text: For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty

timothy-turned-unto-fables.text: For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears; And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables

psalm-heathen-are-come-into-thine-inheri.text: O god, the heathen are come into thine inheritance; thy holy temple have they defiled; they have laid Jerusalem on heaps. The dead bodies of thy servants have they given to be meat unto the fowls of the heaven, the flesh of thy saints unto the beasts of the earth. Their blood have they shed like water round about Jerusalem; and there was none to bury them. We are become a reproach to our neighbours, a scorn and derision to them that are round about us

isaiah-your-hands-are-full-of-blood.text: And when ye spread forth your hands, I will hide mine eyes from you: yea, when ye make many prayers, I will not hear: your hands are full of blood

malachi-priests-lips-should-keep-knowled.text: For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the Lord of hosts. But ye are departed out of the way; ye have caused many to stumble at the law; ye have corrupted the covenant of Levi, saith the Lord of hosts

luke-build-the-sepulchres-of-the-prophet.text: Woe unto you! for ye build the sepulchres of the prophets, and your fathers killed them. Truly ye bear witness that ye allow the deeds of your fathers: for they indeed killed them, and ye build their sepulchres

quran-sons-of-allah-and-his-loved-ones.text: The Jews and Christians say: We are sons of Allah and His loved ones. Say: Why then doth He chastise you for your sins? Nay, ye are but mortals of His creating. He forgiveth whom He will, and chastiseth whom He will. Allah's is the Sovereignty of the heavens and the earth and all that is between them, and unto Him is the journeying.

quran-jews-say-christians-follow-nothing.text: And the Jews say the Christians follow nothing (true), and the Christians say the Jews follow nothing (true); yet both are readers of the Scripture. Even thus speak those who know not. Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they differ.

quran-sunder-their-religion-no-concern.text: Lo! As for those who sunder their religion and become schismatics, no concern at all hast thou with them. Their case will go to Allah, Who then will tell them what they used to do.

quran-then-long-for-death.text: Say (O Muhammad): O ye who are Jews! If ye claim that ye are favoured of Allah apart from (all) mankind, then long for death if ye are truthful.

quran-not-in-accordance-with-your-desire.text: It will not be in accordance with your desires, nor the desires of the People of the Scripture. He who doeth wrong will have the recompense thereof, and will not find against Allah any protecting friend or helper.

quran-a-people-who-have-passed-away.text: Those are a people who have passed away. Theirs is that which they earned, and yours is that which ye earn. And ye will not be asked of what they used to do.

quran-allah-is-not-unjust-they-wrong-the.text: Lo! Allah wrongeth not mankind in aught; but mankind wrong themselves.
